name: pgl (Pangolin plane geometry library)
baseline: CGAL 6.1.2 (Delaunay_triangulation_2, convex_hull_2, Kd_tree, AABB_tree, Arrangement_2, General_polygon_set_2, minkowski_sum_2; EPECK and EPICK kernels)
workload: Wall-clock time of 2D computational-geometry problems (triangulation, convex hull, kd-tree/AABB search, segment intersection, arrangements, polygon unions, Minkowski sum, visibility) on identical integer-coordinate inputs, pgl number type vs the comparable CGAL kernel, across input sizes up to the dataset limits (random data plus Salzburg polygon database).
claimed_speedup: Ratios are pgl time / CGAL time (below 1 = pgl faster), median over sizes. ERational vs EPECK: segment intersection 0.55x (0.19-1.8), regularized union of triangles 0.23x (0.20-0.59), arrangement point-location query 0.46x (0.32-0.84), segment search count in Rectangle 0.68x, nearest neighbor query 0.82x. int vs EPICK: segment search count in Triangle 0.21x, segment intersection 0.35x, count in Rectangle 0.51x, convex hull 0.51x. CGAL is faster on Delaunay triangulation (pgl 2.6x slower ERational/EPECK, 1.7x slower int/EPICK), triangulation point location, Minkowski sum and kd-tree build. Overall ERational/EPECK spans CGAL 2.6x faster to pgl 4.4x faster; int/EPICK spans CGAL 1.8x faster to pgl 4.8x faster.
hardware: Two machines, one run each; CPU models not stated in doc/cgal.md
tradeoffs: Plane-only (2D) library; no higher dimensions, curved geometry, straight skeletons/offsets, alpha shapes or file formats. Header-only, needs C++20 or newer (tested GCC 13, Clang 18, MSVC). Fixed short list of number types, no filtered-kernel layer.
caveats: First-party comparison with partial methodology (CPU model not stated), so tier C. The README itself says pgl is tuned against this benchmark. Mixed result: CGAL wins Delaunay triangulation, convex hull (ERational), Minkowski sum and some builds. Some rows favor pgl by construction (CGAL Kd_tree has no triangle query, so the benchmark wrote one). Ratios are averaged over two machines. Only a small number of the rows are clear pgl wins; do not read it as a blanket CGAL replacement.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch '"faster than CGAL" benchmark github Delaunay OR convex hull OR kd-tree OR polygon' surfaced gfonsecabr/pgl

name: geo-index (packed immutable R-tree and k-d tree)
workload: Criterion benchmark on one bounding-box dataset (benches/bounds.raw): bulk construction of an R-tree from boxes, and a bounding-box search, geo-index (Hilbert-sorted packed tree) vs rstar::RTree::bulk_load.
claimed_speedup: README: construction is ~2x faster than rstar and search is ~33% faster. Numbers: construction geo-index hilbert 80.891 ms vs rstar bulk 159.34 ms; STRTree 116.52 ms; search 116.41 us (flatbush-style) vs rstar 153.62 us; with the rayon feature STRTree construction drops to 72.099 ms.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench rtree (Criterion); rustc version, profile and flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 200 stars; used under the hood in geoarrow-rs
tradeoffs: Trees are immutable (no insert or delete after build), fully packed single-buffer layout with ABI-stable memory shared with Python and the flatbush/kdbush JavaScript libraries. Hilbert and STR sort methods. Also ships a k-d tree.
caveats: Author says it is just one benchmark and recommends benchmarking on your own data. Hardware, dataset size and compiler settings are not stated. Comparing a static packed index against a dynamic R-tree's bulk load is not like-for-like on features (rstar supports updates). Search is a single fixed bounding-box query on one dataset (the bench labels geo-index runs 'flatbush' because the tree is a Rust port of the flatbush packed Hilbert R-tree), so the 33% figure rests on one query.
found_via: GitHub: topic spatial-index / WebSearch 'faster than GEOS' Rust geometry library; README of kylebarron/geo-index

name: qdgeo
baseline: GEOS 3.13.1 (via Shapely 2.1.2): union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference and buffer
workload: 26 boolean/buffer workloads over a 4,040-parcel, 135,080-coordinate public county parcel dataset (GeoMoose demo data); each figure is median of three suite runs of 11 repeats.
claimed_speedup: README: full-dataset parcel union is 3.1x native GEOS (qdgeo wasm 160 ms, qdgeo native 130 ms vs GEOS 426 ms for 4,040 parcels; 1,000 parcels 20.3 / 16.8 ms vs 65.7 ms). Geometric mean over the 26 workloads: GEOS native 1.5x slower than qdgeo wasm (range across runs 1.36-1.62). Buffer of 100 parcels +2 m: 1.30 ms vs GEOS 4.54 ms. GEOS is faster on a single 19,208-coordinate parcel buffer (8.25 ms vs 33.2 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, zig build native -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe (shipped build keeps safety checks); WASM build run in Node 22+
hardware: One idle machine; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Only five operations (four booleans and rounded buffer). Rejects invalid geometry instead of repairing it, and valid input can occasionally fail (4 of 3,946 cluster unions) because it declines to snap coordinates. WASM artifact 135 KB raw, 50.8 KB gzipped, no C or C++ dependency; Zig native build has a C-compatible ABI.
caveats: Application-level comparison: the README admits boundaries are not equal. GEOS runs on already-built geometry objects via shapely.union_all (no parse/encode) while qdgeo rows include WKB codec cost, which favors GEOS; but GEOS is native and qdgeo also reports a native column. The README says to treat gaps under 20% as unresolved. GEOS is faster on very large single polygons. Project is days old. Not a general GEOS replacement. CPU model missing so tier C.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'Rust OR C++ geometry library "faster than GEOS" OR "outperforms GEOS" benchmark'

name: GeoRepair (geo-repair)
baseline: GEOS 3.14.1 (conda-forge libgeos, MSVC build) makeValid / UnaryUnion
workload: Validation and repair (ST_MakeValid equivalent) of 1,579,030 polygon parts from a production GeoPackage, plus synthetic cases (valid polygons, bowties, collapsed rings, near-collinear, large coordinates, linestrings) of 4 to 10,000 vertices; parallel batch.
claimed_speedup: Real-world dataset (README): validation 2.1 s (1.3 us/poly) vs GEOS 3.0 s (1.9 us/poly), 1.4x; full pass 3.6 s vs 3.0 s (0.83x, GEOS faster). docs/BENCHMARKS.md table: validation 2.47 s vs 3.46 s (1.40x), full pass 4.05 s vs 3.49 s (0.86x). Synthetic: valid polygon 4v 4.8x, invalid bowtie 4v 25x, bowtie 1000v 8.0x, collapsed 1000v 5.5x, zero-length line 45x. GEOS faster on large valid polygons (10000v 0.37x), spaghetti (0.56x) and large coordinates 1e12 (0.08x at 1000v).
compiler_and_flags: Rust release profile: lto=fat, codegen-units=1, mimalloc, Rust edition 2024 (rust-version 1.88); GEOS conda-forge 3.14.1 MSVC, no LTO
tradeoffs: Specialised to geometry validation and repair, not a general GEOS replacement. Rayon parallel batch API; Structure strategy mirrors GEOS ST_MakeValid, Arrange strategy is a CDT fallback. Built-in WKB/WKT/batch I/O. Passes the GEOS XML validation suite per README.
caveats: Mixed results: GeoRepair loses on large valid polygons, spaghetti geometry, large coordinates and on the full real-world pass. GeoRepair column is a 12-thread Rayon batch while GEOS is serial per call driven concurrently via Rayon in the same process. README history note: earlier GEOS columns went through a WKT round trip that inflated wins 30-500x; the current harness builds geometry directly. First-party benchmark. Sub-microsecond rows are dispatch noise per the authors.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'Rust OR C++ geometry library "faster than GEOS" OR "outperforms GEOS" benchmark'

name: PicoTree
baseline: nanoflann v1.7.1 kd-tree (also SciPy KDTree, scikit-learn KDTree, pykdtree, OpenCV FLANN)
workload: Kd-tree build and 1-NN query on two LiDAR point clouds of 7,733,372 (build) and 7,200,863 (query) points, single thread, max_leaf_size=10, knn=1.
claimed_speedup: README table: build C++ nanoflann 1.42 s vs PicoTree 0.54 s; knn C++ nanoflann 1.40 s vs PicoTree 1.13 s; OpenCV FLANN build 0.99 s, knn 2.30 s; Python build SciPy 1.37 s, scikit-learn 3.60 s, pykdtree 0.43 s vs PicoTree 0.54 s; Python knn SciPy 212.04 s, scikit-learn 11.90 s, pykdtree 2.95 s vs PicoTree 1.64 s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README table; docs/benchmark.md says an older comparison used MinGW GCC 10.3 (PicoTree 0.7.4 vs nanoflann 1.3.2)
tradeoffs: Static kd-tree (no incremental updates); header-only C++ with optional pybind11 Python bindings; Eigen and OpenCV interop; non-Euclidean metrics (SO2, SE2).
caveats: Compiler and flags missing for the current table so the evidence is first-party tier C; benchmark code is public (examples/benchmark). nanoflann is not in this category's baseline list and is already catalogued. Nanoflann 1-NN query is only about 1.2x slower; the main win is build time (2.6x). docs/benchmark.md notes nanoflann 1.5.0 build regressed ~90% in an older comparison. Kd-tree competitors only, not Boost.Geometry or CGAL.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'spatial index faster than R-tree benchmark github C++ library' follow-up; README of Jaybro/pico_tree

name: geo-utils-cpp
baseline: Boost.Geometry 1.90.0 spherical strategies (bg::area, bg::within, bg::distance); also S2 Geometry 0.14.0 and GeographicLib 2.7
workload: Google Benchmark throughput of lat/lng spherical operations (distance, heading, point-in-polygon, polygon area, path length) on seeded random data with native types pre-built outside the timed loop.
claimed_speedup: Polygon area (N=100 vertices): 67.2 M polygons/s vs Boost.Geometry 36.2 (N=10: 69.9 vs 45.0; N=1000: 67.7 vs 36.6), roughly 1.5-1.9x (derived from page data). Point-in-polygon (contains): 16.2 / 2.87 / 0.329 M queries/s vs Boost.Geometry 1.91 / 0.234 / 0.024 at N=10/100/1000 (roughly 8-14x; algorithms differ). distance_between ties Boost.Geometry (40.5 vs 39.8 M pairs/s); S2 is faster on distance, contains and path_length.
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 17, -std=c++17 -O2 -DNDEBUG, Release, Google Benchmark 1.8.4; boost 1.90.0, s2geometry 0.14.0, geographiclib 2.7
hardware: Apple M1, 8 cores, 8 GB RAM, macOS 15.7
tradeoffs: Spherical Earth model only (mean radius 6371009 m), not WGS84 ellipsoid; precision degrades near poles and for antipodal pairs. Narrow feature set (distance, bearing, area, point-in-polygon, path proximity, Google polyline). No spatial indexing. Header-only, no dependencies, C++17.
caveats: The contains comparison is not like-for-like: geo-utils-cpp uses a rhumb-line ray cast (geodesic=false default) while Boost.Geometry within uses a great-circle spherical winding strategy, so the gap partly reflects algorithm choice. The only clear Boost.Geometry win on equal work is polygon area (~1.5-1.9x); distance, heading and path_length are ties within noise. S2 beats it on contains and path_length. Single machine, first-party benchmark, repository created May 2026.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github C++ "point in polygon" SIMD faster than GEOS OR Boost.Geometry OR CGAL benchmark'

name: Delaunay32
workload: 2D Delaunay triangulation of one million unique unconstrained signed 32-bit integer points, triangle-only output, runtime in ms.
claimed_speedup: README table: Delaunay32 45.4 ms (8 threads) and 131.6 ms (1 thread) vs Fade2D 235.2 ms (automatic threads) / 314.1 ms (1 thread), delaunator-cpp 542.0 ms, Triangle 1.6 584.0 ms, CDT 1.4.5 988.7 ms (all single thread). Relative runtime: 1 thread Delaunay32 2.9x vs 8 threads; Triangle 12.9x, delaunator-cpp 11.9x, CDT 21.8x of the 8-thread time.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build; compiler and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Accepts only signed 32-bit integer coordinates (floating-point input must go through the explicit quantize() utility, with collision/error report); exact integer predicates; supports constraints and polygon domains with holes; optional multithreading; WebAssembly package exists.
caveats: First-party single-machine result with compiler and flags missing, so tier C. Baselines are Triangle, Fade2D, delaunator-cpp and CDT, not CGAL, so baseline_in_list is false (Triangle is the classic incumbent). Inputs are integer points, which favors an exact-integer design versus double-coordinate libraries that must run floating-point robust predicates. Single-thread comparison is 131.6 ms vs Triangle 584.0 ms (4.4x, derived from page data). The repo is very new.

name: Hob3l
baseline: OpenSCAD with CGAL rendering (CGAL Nef polyhedron 3D CSG) converting SCAD/CSG to STL
workload: Converting Prusa i3 MK3 part and personal SCAD models to STL by slicing into 0.2 mm layers (Hob3l) versus full 3D CSG rendering in OpenSCAD with CGAL.
claimed_speedup: README: x-carriage.csg to STL 45.208 s (openscad) vs 0.824 s (hob3l), about 50x faster; extruder-body.scad 2m42s vs 1.24 s, 130x; uselessbox+body 53.433 s vs 0.610 s, 85x. test31b.scad ($fn=99 ellipsoids) 4m30.198s vs 0.748s, 350x. Repo title says '100x Faster Slicing of SCAD Files'.
tradeoffs: Different pipeline, not a general CGAL replacement: it slices the model into 2D layers and does 2D boolean operations with integer arithmetic and snap rounding, so output is a layered STL (visible layering artifacts) rather than an exact 3D mesh. Reads flat .csg from OpenSCAD plus STL/SVG import. GPL-3.0.
caveats: Wall-clock `time` figures on unspecified hardware and flags; speedups above 50x reflect a different algorithm and a lower-fidelity output, so they are not like-for-like with CGAL mesh booleans. Baseline is OpenSCAD's CGAL rendering path, not CGAL used directly. Last commit June 2024.
found_via: GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/polygon-clipping listed moehriegitt/hob3l ('100x Faster Slicing of SCAD Files')

name: CavalierContours (C++)
baseline: Clipper (Angus Johnson Clipper1 polygon offsetting, rounded joins)
workload: Repeated inward and outward offsets of 2D polylines with arcs (square, circle, rounded rectangle, two small profiles, pathological alternating-arc circles of 10-100 half circles) with increasing delta, wall time in ms.
claimed_speedup: README tables (cavc vs Clipper, arcs approximated 1e-2): square 0.21 vs 0.72 ms (3.5x), pathological/100 336.37 vs 1347.09 ms (4.0x); Profile1 8.55 vs 6.33 ms (0.7x, Clipper faster). Arcs approximated 1e-3: pathological/100 821.15 vs 15797.60 ms (19.2x), square 8.1x. With exact arcs: circle 0.12 vs 9.47 ms (76.4x), pathological/10 1.61 vs 136.46 ms (84.9x), vs Clipper 1e-3 circle 494.7x, pathological/10 861.0x.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2019 19.24.28314 targeting 64-bit (MinGW 7.3 64-bit gave similar results); optimization flags not stated; Clipper input scaled by 1e8 to 64-bit integers
tradeoffs: Handles 2D polylines with constant-radius arc segments natively (exact arcs rather than line-segment approximation); supports offsetting, boolean operations, header-only C++14 with C API. Not a general polygon library.
caveats: Author states the C++ library is no longer actively developed; development moved to the Rust crate cavalier_contours (dual MIT/Apache-2.0 with a C FFI). The huge ratios come from exact-arc offsets versus Clipper's line-segment approximation, so they are partly a representation advantage; with arcs converted to segments the win is 0.7x-19x and Clipper wins on Profile1. Benchmarks are hardware from about 2020, compiler flags unspecified. Clipper is not in the category baseline list.
found_via: GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/spatial-index listed jbuckmccready/CavalierContours (2D polyline offsetting)

name: fastquadtree
baseline: Rtree (Python wrapper of libspatialindex R-tree) and Shapely STRtree (GEOS); also PyQtree and other Python quadtrees
workload: Build 500,000 points and run 500 range queries; total time per library, Python spatial indexes (bounds 0-1000, max 128 points per node, max depth 16).
claimed_speedup: docs/benchmark.md: total time fastquadtree (numpy path) 0.068 s (build 0.052 s, query 0.017 s), fastquadtree list path 0.285 s, Shapely STRtree 0.309 s, Rtree 2.351 s (build 1.805 s, query 0.546 s), PyQtree 2.909 s. About 34x faster total than Rtree with the numpy path (derived from page data), 8.2x with the list path; 42.52x vs PyQtree. Drop-in pyqtree shim 11.647 s vs 1.127 s (10.3x).
compiler_and_flags: CPython 3.14.5; Rust engine built via PyO3/maturin (release flags not stated in the benchmark page)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (16 threads), 31.3 GB RAM, CachyOS Linux
tradeoffs: Python package with a Rust core; point and rectangle quadtree with numpy bulk paths, optional object tracking, serialization to bytes. Quadtree rather than R-tree: no balanced bulk-loading guarantees.
caveats: First-party Python benchmark; the best number uses the numpy return path while the list path (comparable to Rtree's list returns) is much slower. Shapely STRtree row uses numpy points and returns. Rust compiler flags not stated. Query count is only 500. Workload is point data, not extended geometries.
found_via: GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/spatial-index?page=2 listed Elan456/fastquadtree

name: RBush
workload: 1M uniformly distributed rectangles of ~0.01% area, maxEntries 16: one-by-one insert, searches of 0.01%, 1% and 10% area, one-by-one removal, bulk insert.
claimed_speedup: README table (RBush vs old RTree): insert 1M items one by one 3.18 s vs 7.83 s (2.5x); 1000 searches of 0.01% area 0.03 s vs 0.93 s (30x); 1% area 0.35 s vs 2.27 s (6.5x); 10% area 2.18 s vs 9.53 s (4.4x); remove 1000 items 0.02 s vs 1.18 s (50x); bulk-insert 1M items 1.25 s (6.7x, no bulk insert in the old library).
hardware: Retina MacBook Pro 15 (mid-2012); CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: 2D only; R-tree with OMT bulk loading and STLT bulk insertion, R*-tree style split; mutable (insert, remove). README recommends kdbush (static points) and Flatbush (static rectangles) for faster static indexes.
caveats: Numbers are from Node 6.2.2 on a 2012 laptop and compare against an old JavaScript R-tree, not against a C/C++ library or Boost.Geometry; benchmark script is public but hardware CPU model is missing. Baseline is another R-tree implementation, so it is evidence of algorithm tuning rather than a win over a major incumbent.
found_via: GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/spatial-index (top repository by stars)

name: KDBush
workload: Static 2D point indexing (flat KD-tree in one array buffer) versus RBush R-tree point indexing and range/radius queries.
claimed_speedup: RBush README: 'kdbush ... performs point indexing 5-8x faster than RBush'. KDBush README: 'Faster indexing and search, with lower memory footprint' versus RBush, with no numbers in the text.
tradeoffs: Points only (no rectangles), static (cannot add or remove after indexing), single ArrayBuffer storage; Flatbush is the rectangle equivalent and KDBush uses about 2x less memory than Flatbush for points.
caveats: The 5-8x figure is a one-line claim in RBush's README with no workload, hardware or code reference; the kdbush repo has a bench.js but publishes no numbers. Compared against a JavaScript R-tree, not a native library.
found_via: GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/spatial-index listed mourner/kdbush; claim read in mourner/rbush README

name: Indexicon R-tree
workload: R-tree insertion time and range-query time on six datasets (MARINE, MIAMI, OSM, TAXIS, TIGER, TORONTO) for node capacities 32 to 512.
claimed_speedup: README only shows figures (figures/rtree_insert_time.png, rtree_query_time.png), no numbers in text. Read from the figures (approximate): query time e.g. MARINE node capacity 32 about 280 ms vs Boost about 425 ms, capacity 64 about 225 vs 328 ms; TORONTO capacity 32 about 30 vs 39 ms; insertion typically 5-20% faster (e.g. MARINE capacity 512 about 25 s vs 32 s); on OSM at capacity 32 and TIGER at 128 the two are close to equal. (derived from figure reading)
compiler_and_flags: Example build line g++ -std=c++17 -O2; benchmark compiler and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Single-header R-tree (point and MBB variants), quadtree, MX-CIF quadtree, octree and kd-tree with unified API; R-tree has top-down packing, R* insertion, and deletion that dissolves sparse nodes; any dimension.
caveats: Claim is graphical only; the comprehensive benchmark is in an arXiv paper (2606.04676) that could not be opened from this container. No hardware, compiler flags or Boost version stated for the R-tree figures. Gains over Boost are modest (about 1.0-1.5x), largest on query time at small node capacities.

name: SPRK-tree (Sorted Projection Radius KD-tree)
baseline: CGAL kd-tree, Boost.Geometry R-tree and nanoflann kd-tree (benchmarked as optional backends in the rembed harness, alongside Kiddo, SIF, VP-tree, grid, quadtree)
workload: Radius queries (and nearest neighbor queries) on graph embeddings and other point sets, up to 10M points and 2 to 960 dimensions, from the ESA 2026 paper 'Benchmarking and Engineering Data Structures for Spherical Range Queries'.
claimed_speedup: No numeric speedup read: the paper could not be opened from this container (arxiv.org and dagstuhl blocked). Search-result summary of the paper abstract: the SPRK-tree achieves the fastest query times in almost all benchmarks and ranks second in the few remaining ones.
compiler_and_flags: README advises RUSTFLAGS -Ctarget-cpu=native (AVX-512 compress when available); full flags in paper not read
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; crate published as sprk on crates.io
tradeoffs: Radius queries in D-dimensional Euclidean space; SIMD leaf scans with lookup-table pruning, SVD projection for D > 16, parallel construction, update() rebuild that reuses allocations. Not a general spatial index (no rectangles or nearest-neighbor guarantees in the README).
caveats: Peer-reviewed (ESA 2026 LIPIcs) but numbers were not verified here: the paper and its tables were unreachable, and neither the sprk nor rembed README quotes speedups. Evidence tier B is on the strength of the paper plus public benchmark harness (rembed with reproducibility-cli). Verifier should open the paper for numbers, CPU and flags. Benchmarks target embeddings from graph drawing, with many high-dimensional cases.
